## Part 1 — Setup and Cleaning

```{python}
try:
    with open("pride_and_prejudice.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        book1_lines = f.readlines()

    with open("frankenstein.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        book2_lines = f.readlines()

    print("Pride and Prejudice:", len(book1_lines), "lines")
    print("Frankenstein:", len(book2_lines), "lines")

except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Couldn't find a book file. Check its name and location.")
```

```{python}
while not book1_lines[0].startswith("*** START"):
    book1_lines = book1_lines[1:]

book1_lines = book1_lines[1:]

while not book1_lines[-1].startswith("*** END"):
    book1_lines = book1_lines[:-1]

book1_lines = book1_lines[:-1]

print(book1_lines[:5])
print(book1_lines[-5:])
```

```{python}
while not book2_lines[0].startswith("*** START"):
    book2_lines = book2_lines[1:]

book2_lines = book2_lines[1:]

while not book2_lines[-1].startswith("*** END"):
    book2_lines = book2_lines[:-1]

book2_lines = book2_lines[:-1]

print(book2_lines[:5])
print(book2_lines[-5:])
```

```{python}
import re

book1_text = "".join(book1_lines).lower()
book2_text = "".join(book2_lines).lower()

book1_words = re.split(r"[\W]+", book1_text)
book2_words = re.split(r"[\W]+", book2_text)

book1_words = [w for w in book1_words if w != ""]
book2_words = [w for w in book2_words if w != ""]

print(book1_words[:10])
print(book2_words[:10])
```

I opened the 2 books and used .readlines() to save each book as a list of lines. I then used while loops to remove many of the first line and last lines until they reacehd the markers. After, I removed the markers. I joined the other lines that were left and made the text lowercase. I used re.split() to separate it into words. Then I removed the empty strings. I used ChatGPT to understand how to use "while" and fix a file-path problem.



## Part 2 — Tokens, Types, and a Fair Comparison

```{python}
book1_tokens = len(book1_words)
book2_tokens = len(book2_words)

book1_types = len(set(book1_words))
book2_types = len(set(book2_words))

book1_ttr = book1_types / book1_tokens
book2_ttr = book2_types / book2_tokens

print("Pride and Prejudice")
print("Tokens:", book1_tokens)
print("Types:", book1_types)
print("Full-book TTR:", book1_ttr)

print("Frankenstein")
print("Tokens:", book2_tokens)
print("Types:", book2_types)
print("Full-book TTR:", book2_ttr)
```

```{python}
book1_sample = book1_words[:10000]
book2_sample = book2_words[:10000]

book1_sample_ttr = len(set(book1_sample)) / len(book1_sample)
book2_sample_ttr = len(set(book2_sample)) / len(book2_sample)

print("Pride and Prejudice — first 10,000 words TTR:", book1_sample_ttr)
print("Frankenstein — first 10,000 words TTR:", book2_sample_ttr)
```

```{python}
book1_total_length = 0

for word in book1_words:
    book1_total_length += len(word)

book1_average_length = book1_total_length / book1_tokens

book2_total_length = 0

for word in book2_words:
    book2_total_length += len(word)

book2_average_length = book2_total_length / book2_tokens

print("Pride and Prejudice — average word length:", book1_average_length)
print("Frankenstein — average word length:", book2_average_length)
```
I used len() to count the tokens and len(set()) to count the types with no duplicates. Then calculated TTR dividing types by tokens. Frankenstein had the higher TTR of the books and the first 10,000 words. Comparing 10,000 words from both books is more fair because the texts are the same length, so it reduces the effect of text length on TTR. For the calculation of the average word length, I used a loop to add each word's length and divided the total by the number of the words. The average word lengths were almost the same. I used AI to troubleshoot the error when I left out necesary parenthesis and to check I correctly used only the 10,000 words of each book.


## Part 3 — Affixes, Dialogue, and Common Words

```{python}
book1_ly = [w for w in book1_words if w.endswith("ly")]
book2_ly = [w for w in book2_words if w.endswith("ly")]

book1_ly_rate = len(book1_ly) / len(book1_words) * 1000
book2_ly_rate = len(book2_ly) / len(book2_words) * 1000

print("Pride and Prejudice — ly words per 1,000:", book1_ly_rate)
print("Frankenstein — ly words per 1,000:", book2_ly_rate)

print(book1_ly[:30])
print(book2_ly[:30])
```

```{python}
book1_ness = [w for w in book1_words if w.endswith("ness")]
```

```{python}
book1_nonempty = [line for line in book1_lines if line.strip() != ""]
book2_nonempty = [line for line in book2_lines if line.strip() != ""]

book1_dialogue = [
    line for line in book1_nonempty
    if '"' in line or '“' in line or '‘' in line
]

book2_dialogue = [
    line for line in book2_nonempty
    if '"' in line or '“' in line or '‘' in line
]

book1_dialogue_percent = len(book1_dialogue) / len(book1_nonempty) * 100
book2_dialogue_percent = len(book2_dialogue) / len(book2_nonempty) * 100

print("Pride and Prejudice — dialogue lines (%):", book1_dialogue_percent)
print("Frankenstein — dialogue lines (%):", book2_dialogue_percent)

print(book1_dialogue[:3])
print(book2_dialogue[:3])
```

```{python}
from collections import Counter

stopwords = [
    "the", "to", "and", "of", "a", "her", "i", "in", "was", "it",
    "she", "he", "be", "that", "you", "not", "had", "as", "his", "for",
    "with", "is", "have", "but", "at", "so", "all", "my", "been", "him",
    "on", "by", "could", "would", "very", "no", "what", "which", "they",
    "were", "there", "me", "an", "must", "this", "said", "from", "or",
    "will", "any", "much", "than", "such", "their", "them", "if", "do",
    "did", "one", "when", "your", "more", "are", "we", "who", "up",
    "out", "down", "into", "s", "t"
]

stopwords = stopwords + [
    "mr", "mrs", "miss", "am", "should", "now", "these",
    "yet", "some", "before", "myself",
    "has", "though", "herself", "how", "upon", "our",
    "its", "only", "every", "then"
]

book1_content = [w for w in book1_words if w not in stopwords]
book2_content = [w for w in book2_words if w not in stopwords]

book1_counts = Counter(book1_content)
book2_counts = Counter(book2_content)

print("Pride and Prejudice:", book1_counts.most_common(10))
print("Frankenstein:", book2_counts.most_common(10))
```
I used .endswith() and .startswith() to find words ending in ly, ness, and ment and words starting with un. I divided the counts by the total words and multiplied it by 1000 to compare the books fairly like in part 2. Austen had words ending in ly and ment, while Shelley had more words ending with ness and starting with un. The ly words weren't all adverbs becuase there were words like fly and reply as well. I also removed blank lines and counted the lines with quotationmarks. Pride and Prejudice had about 13.95% and Frankenstein had about 6.84%. I used the stopword list from the slides and added more words on after seeing the results. Then I used counter and .most_common(10) to find the most common words left. Austen's results had names of the characters in the book like Elizabeth and Darcy. Shelley's had words like man, father, and life which suggest topcis about people and family. I used ChatGPT to help decide what extra stopwords to use after seeing how common the words still looked after using the stop list from the class slides.


## Part 4 — Visualize It

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.bar(["Jane Austen", "Mary Shelley"],
        [book1_ly_rate, book2_ly_rate])

plt.title("Words Ending in -ly")
plt.xlabel("Author")
plt.ylabel("Matches per 1,000 words")
plt.savefig("ly_comparison.png")
plt.show()
```
```{python}
book1_freqs = [pair[1] for pair in Counter(book1_words).most_common()]
book2_freqs = [pair[1] for pair in Counter(book2_words).most_common()]

book1_ranks = range(1, len(book1_freqs) + 1)
book2_ranks = range(1, len(book2_freqs) + 1)

plt.plot(book1_ranks, book1_freqs, label="Jane Austen")
plt.plot(book2_ranks, book2_freqs, label="Mary Shelley")

plt.title("Word Rank vs. Frequency")
plt.xlabel("Rank")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.xscale("log")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("zipf_comparison.png")
plt.show()
```
I used matplotlib to make a bar chart comparing ly words for both authors. The author names are the labels, and the rates from part 3 are the heights of the bars. For the Zipf plot, I used counter to put all the words in order from most common to least common. I used pair[1] to get each word's count and range() to create the ranks. I plotted both books on the same graph and made both axes log scales. I added titles, labels, and a legend and used .savefig() to save both charts. I used ChatGPT to help me fully understand how to use log with the charts.

## Part 5 — The Verdict
Like I previously mentioned Austen had higher rates of words ending in ly and ment, while Shelley had higher rates of words ending in ness and words starting with un. Austen's common words had characters names like Darcy and Elizabeth while Shelley's included man, father, and life. I think the ly rate was the most useful because there was a noticeable difference between the books. Average word length was the least useful because the results were almost the same. If I had an anonymous chapter, I would check the ly rate first, but I would need more evidence before deciding who wrote it.
